process: D20: two blind graders (D7), adjudicator on disagreements, agent audit of agreed verdicts (D11)

verdicts.reason: A measure exists, so not ungradable: enterprise mobile e-mail is counted by RIM's BlackBerry subscriber series and mobile data use by Ofcom. BlackBerry subscribers doubled each year (534,000 FY2003, 1.07m FY2004, 2.51m FY2005), so business take-up did accelerate, but business mobile data stayed a small share in 2004: non-SMS data was 2% of UK mobile retail revenue. Measurable but below mainstream by the placed year; routine business use came 3 to 5 years later. Grader A's partial stands.

Graders' key fact (FCC 'granted many' Phase II waivers) is not on the cited Wikipedia 'Enhanced 911' page, which instead says many phones made after 2005 have built-in GPS and the 95% location-capable handset deadline was end-2005 (some carriers fined). The forecast (pressure for faster, cheaper location 'right across the world') is met in the US by about 2005 (3 years: partial) but not worldwide (miss); the evidence does not settle which, so no verdict is supported.

The claim is about a trend in handset size, so it needs a size or weight series by year. Grader A's single model (Nokia 7650, 154 g, June 2002) is one flagship, not the trend; slim and small models kept launching (Motorola T720 2002, RAZR 2004). The only series found (USGS citing Environmental Literacy Council and Nokia) gives a typical phone at 218 g in 2000 and 113 g in 2005, but the 2005 figure excludes the battery and the 2000 figure's basis is not stated, so it cannot show whether the curve flattened in 2002. No consistent public series reached: ungradable (D22/D23).

The sentence is framed as what users 'must be prepared' to accept, but the chapter's headline 'Swap privacy for security' is a forecast that the swap happens, and it has a dated observable: the EU ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC (adopted July 2002) obliges providers to erase traffic data unless Article 15(1) conditions apply, which let member states require retention for security and crime purposes; retention was later made mandatory by the Data Retention Directive (2006), which amends 2002/58. The swap was written into law in the target year. Grader B's normative-only reading ignores the headline. Low-medium confidence: the claim is soft.

The claim is a revival, not mainstream status. The revival happened: Vodafone live! (colour-handset portal, launched October 2002) had 1 million customers by April 2003 and 1.5 million by May 2003, and WAP 'made a stronger resurgence' in 2003-2004 with Vodafone live! and T-Mobile T-Zones. Grader A's Ofcom evidence (mobile internet 'relatively insignificant' in 2004) shows WAP stayed small, which tests a claim of significance that Deloitte did not make. Hit.

The headline is about data growth, and it slowed: Ofcom's UK mobile retail revenue shows SMS plus data at £1.4bn (2002), £1.9bn (2003), £2.1bn (2004), so growth fell from about 36% to about 11%; SMS revenue rose only from £1.8bn to £1.9bn; the average SMS sent per subscriber was unchanged in 2004; MMS and mobile internet stayed small. Grader B is right that total UK text volumes kept growing (over 28bn in 2004), but that growth came from more subscriptions; the forecast's mechanism (SMS deceleration not offset by other data) held. UK is the only market checked, so medium confidence.

A public assessment of exactly this exists: Ofcom's 2005 review headed its section 'WiFi hotspots are growing in number, but usage is still low', noting roaming-inflated site counts, substantial price cuts in 2004 and packages still aimed at corporate users. No hourly utilisation series exists, but the regulator's measure of usage supports the claim. Hit, medium confidence.

No developed-market-only figure was found, but the global series brackets it: ABI put colour screens at nearly 38% of all handsets sold in 2003, and iSuppli at 74% of handset main displays in 2005. Developed markets led the switch (IDC, January 2004: North American and Western European buyers were ditching monochrome phones), and the global figure is pulled down by low-end emerging-market sales, so the developed-market share was above 50% by end-2004 on any interpolation. Polyphony shipped on colour phones from 2002 (Nokia 3510 onward). Hit, medium confidence (inference from the global series).

The edition settles grader B's two readings: the chapter defines 'indirectly on usage' as speed tiers, not volume caps. Speed-tiered broadband became standard (Ofcom 2006: average price of 512K access fell from £30 to £16 in 2005 while operators sold 'up to 8Mbit/s' packages), and volume caps also arrived in the UK in 2004 (Ofcom 2005), so even the second reading points the same way in the market checked. Not unfalsifiable. Hit.

The claim is about operators' return on hotspot investment. No hotspot revenue or profitability figure for 2004 was found by either grader or the adjudicator. Ofcom's low-usage and price-cut findings make low returns likely, but usage is a proxy of a different quantity (D23), and the adjudicator's prior w1 practice treats such proxies as not a measure. Ungradable; grader A's hit rests on inference.

A measure exists: BT reported 'new wave' turnover (ICT, broadband, mobility) up 32% to £4.47bn in 2004/05, about a quarter of group revenue, with ICT a main driver, and BT Global Services bought Radianz and Infonet in 2005. Grader B did not reach BT's results. Hit; one operator, but the largest European incumbent named in this kind of strategy.

The edition settles the scope (D23: read the scope from the edition): the chapter lists hard drives, smaller/faster processors and storage, sunblock, car tyres and fabrics as the mainstream applications, not nano-labelled consumer gadgets. Nanoscale features were in essentially all new hard drives and processors (90 nm node, GMR heads) by 2005, so at least 50% of new units shipped with it: mainstream at the placed year. Grader A's two readings are therefore not equally faithful; the consumer-product-count reading is not what the chapter says. Grader B's directional test is not the D16 test, but its verdict stands under the D16 test.

The chapter is about household robots starting with the robot vacuum. D16 reads a year placement as mainstream around that year; 'increasingly' does not turn it into a directional claim (grader B's test is not D16). iRobot had sold about 1 million Roombas by 2004 and only about 30 million home robots in total by 2020; robots reached 20% of vacuum-cleaner sales (a flow, not household stock) only in 2016. Household penetration in major markets stayed well under 5% through 2010, so miss, window closed.

ITU: 2,205.3 million mobile-cellular subscriptions in 2005 (checked in the ITU workbook). The captured value is ~2 billion; 2.0bn is 9.3% below the actual, inside the 10% band. Grader B's reading of 'nearly 2 billion' as strictly below 1.985bn is narrower than the captured value; the forecast is graded at its stated number. Hit, at the edge of the band.

The quoted sentence states behaviour, and the behaviour is documented: in 2005 O2 trialled DVB-H TV, BT and Virgin Mobile trialled DAB TV, UK hotspots grew, 3G operators planned HSDPA launches for 2006-2007, and WiMAX was in trials. Whether this spread bets 'too thin' (the headline's judgment) is not graded. Hit.

The edition settles the reading: the chapter says RFID 'in 2005 should make it out of the lab', with retail, defence and automotive mandates prompting 'a massive increase in RFID adoption', then 'by the end of the year, billions ... commissioned'. That is the 2005 flow. IDTechEx counted just over 600 million tags in 2005. Cumulative sales since the 1940s (2.4bn, about 1.8bn before 2005) would make the forecast trivially true and are not what the chapter describes. Grader B's cumulative reading is not equally faithful. 0.6bn against at least 2bn: miss.

The chapter defines the group (fast-growing low-cost providers, especially VoIP and carrier pre-selection entrants) and their growth is measured: by March 2006 there were 6.1 million UK CPS lines, over 40% with Carphone Warehouse (TalkTalk); nearly 34% of UK lines took calls from a provider other than BT; BT's share of all telecoms connections fell from 37% to 26% over five years to 2005, the 'other' category rising from 4% to 12%, mainly CPS and broadband entrants. Hit.

The chapter names its own test: services 'from directory inquiries to tourist information' incorporating natural-language speech recognition, and voice control in vehicles. Both happened inside the D16 two-year window: Google's GOOG-411 speech-recognition directory service launched April 2007, and Ford SYNC voice control (announced January 2007) shipped in twelve 2008-model vehicles in 2007. Grader A's Wii reading is off the chapter's subject and its speech reading asserted 'niche' without evidence; grader B's Wii evidence is also off-subject, but both readings give a hit, so not unfalsifiable.

The definitional gap both graders named is narrower than they thought: the chapter's Figure 3 is titled 'Global console game sales' and sourced to Screen Digest, 'Games Software Publishing - Strategies for Success' (November 2005), so the $23bn is Screen Digest's console game (software) series. No public 2006 actual on that definition was found: Screen Digest figures sit in paid reports; US-only NPD figures and all-platform retail totals (hardware plus software, PC, online) are different quantities (D23). Looked for: Screen Digest 2006/2007 console software press figures, DFC Intelligence, ESA/NPD, PwC outlook. One web search, plus the Deloitte PDF opened. Stays ungradable.

A measure exists, so not ungradable: the US Radio Advertising Bureau tracks 'Off-Air' revenue (mainly online, then experiential marketing). It grew at about 10% a year from mid-2005 and 12.3% over the two years to mid-2008, reaching 9% of US radio revenue, while spot revenue fell. Diversification started, at a measurable share, but the streams the chapter named (paid replays, downloads, subscriptions, premium HD) did not become a significant share, and 9% is below the 20% D16 mainstream line. Grader A's two readings collapse into this one measure. Partial, low-medium confidence (US data only).

Dolce & Gabbana released a limited-edition gold RAZR in December 2005 and another on 1 June 2006; Prada announced its LG-made phone on 12 December 2006, on sale March 2007. The Prada launch falls inside the two-year window D16 allows, so grader B's late-arrival penalty does not apply. Hit.

Measured at a record: per the FCC, US resellers including MVNOs served 15.1 million subscribers at end-2006, up 1.6 million, about 7% of US mobile subscribers. In UK fixed, carrier pre-selection resellers reached 6.1 million lines by March 2006. Grader B's MVNO failures (Mobile ESPN under 10,000 subscribers) are single entrants; the reseller segment grew to its largest size. Hit.

The claim states a state of worry among consumers and businesses. Grader B's evidence (EPA report on data-centre electricity, Aug 2007) shows policy attention to data-centre energy in general; it does not measure consumer or business concern about storage costs, so it is a proxy of another quantity (D23). No 2007 survey of that concern was found by either grader. Ungradable (D22).

By 2007 biometrics were routine in one application, e-passports (EU states, Japan, US from 2005-2007), a measurable share of users. Across the 'large range of applications' the claim names, consumer device use (laptops, phones) became mainstream only after Touch ID in 2013 and its spread to most phones by about 2016-2017, 6 or more years late. Measurable share by the placed year, mainstream across applications not within 2 years: partial. Grader B graded only the passport rollout, which is one application.

The edition text settles grader A's objection: the sentences after the quote are about access to broadband conferring benefits, and the chapter defines the second chasm as between those with broadband 'at a speed and contention ratio sufficient' and those without (under 5% of the world had broadband at the start of 2007); the voice divide in the same chapter is said to be narrowing. ITU: fixed broadband per 100 inhabitants rose from 4.3 (2006) to 5.2 (2007) worldwide while LDCs stayed at about 0, so the gap widened in absolute terms. Hit.

The chapter's subject is the cost burden of spam, spim, spit and malware; the 'suppliers start charging' reading grader A sets against it is a recommendation in the bottom line, not the forecast, so the readings are not equally faithful and unfalsifiable does not apply. Under the chapter's reading the claim needs a cost series for 2006 and 2007; none was found. Spam share of email (about 95% in 2006 per the chapter, 97% in 2008 per Microsoft) is a volume proxy, not a cost (D23). Ungradable.

The chapter expected the 25 member states to introduce country-specific anti-fraud legislation in 2007. The UK did: from 1 June 2007 a VAT reverse charge applied to mobile phones and computer chips, changing invoicing for every supplier of those goods into the UK. EU-wide reverse-charge powers for such goods came only later (quick-reaction and reverse-charge directives around 2010), three years after the placed year. One major market in the year, broader action 3 or more years later: partial. Grader B's 'no measure' ignores the legislative event the chapter names.

The chapter scopes it: 'the technology sector may increasingly adopt a new approach to portable power ... power-scavenging solutions' recharging portable-device batteries. The absence is observable: no phone, laptop or media-player line shipped harvesting as a standard feature in 2007-2012; harvesting stayed in milliwatt niches (sensors, watches, pilot floor tiles). Below 5% within five years: miss. Grader B's lack of a market-size figure does not make it ungradable when no product category adopted it.

An event claim with named examples, and they happened in 2007: the i-LIMB, the first commercial prosthetic hand with individually powered digits, launched in July 2007, and Oscar Pistorius raced non-disabled athletes at Rome's Golden Gala and the British Grand Prix in July 2007, starting the IAAF dispute over his prosthetics. Soft claim, but the chapter's own examples occurred. Hit.

The quality half has no measure, but the threat half does: the largest UGC platform, YouTube, had 2007 revenue Google called 'not material' in its filing, so UGC took no material revenue from media in 2007. Hit.

A measure exists (newspaper revenue, print and online), so not ungradable. But the hedged wording ('may not always be about one versus the other') supports two readings: some publishers profitably combine print and online (true in 2007, when most newspaper groups were still profitable and online revenue grew), or the press as a whole coexists profitably across both (false from 2008, as print revenue collapsed and online did not offset it). The chapter supports both and no reading dominates. Grader A's unfalsifiable stands.

Two faithful readings diverge. On the quoted sentence alone, social networking stayed popular and found a sustainable model on advertising (Facebook EBITDA-profitable early 2008, cash-flow positive September 2009): hit. On the chapter's body, the model would have to lean on subscriptions and paid privacy because 'advertising revenues may not suffice': miss, as advertising won. The quote does not name the model and the chapter does, so neither dominates. Not ungradable: under D23 a necessity claim is graded on its outcome, and the outcome is observable.

Source PDF p14 ties 'primary network for voice' to mobile traffic exceeding PSTN 'in many developed countries'. Evidence: Taiwan crossed in 2007 (Telecompaper, 9 Apr 2008), but the UK was still ~60/40 fixed:mobile in 2007 (3g4g summary of Ofcom 2008) and fixed still led in 2009 (CMR 2010: 133bn vs 118bn); a US crossover could not be verified. One country is too thin for 'many': no verdict supported.

A series exists (ZenithOptimedia global internet adspend), so this is gradable; grader B recorded ungradable only for lack of a retrieved figure. Zenith's later tally for 2008 is about $51.1bn (via Statista), consistent with Zenith's mid-2008 estimate of internet at 10.8% of global adspend in 2008 (roughly $50bn of a total near $480bn). $41.6bn is about 18-19% below: within 25%, not 10%. Deloitte's own base ($41.6bn = +23% implies about $33.8bn in 2007) is lower than Zenith's, a method difference of the same quantity (D23), stated here. The radio comparison held. Partial; one tracker only, medium-low confidence.

Graders graded side figures (tours over $100m). Source PDF pp13-14: the forecast is that recorded music is sold as a physical product again (pre-recorded MP3 players, memory cards, box sets, vinyl). That stayed niche: slotMusic microSD albums (Oct 2008, Wikipedia) did not catch on, and global vinyl trade value was $66m in 2008 and $416m in 2015 (Wikipedia 'Vinyl revival'), under 5% of recorded music, while digital share kept rising (IFPI). Miss.

An event claim, and the year's launches confirm it: Apple's App Store opened 10 July 2008, Spotify launched in Sweden, Finland, France, Norway and Spain on 7 October 2008, Hulu ran as a free online TV service in 2008. Grader B's objection (no threshold) is about strength of the test, not about whether it is observable. Hit.

The quote is one of two scenarios, but the chapter leans: 'service providers may be better able to weather the storm, at least in 2008', 'service revenue growth may hold steady', equipment manufacturers harder hit. Operators' 2008 results held: AT&T revenue $118.9bn (2007) to $124.0bn (2008), net income $11.95bn to $12.87bn; world mobile subscriptions grew by about 660 million. Grader B's stock-price reading is not the chapter's measure (it says operators' stocks 'may be seen as secure', i.e. relative), so the operating reading dominates. Hit, medium confidence.

A measure exists, so not ungradable: Berg Insight counts cellular M2M connections (81.4 million at end-2010, up 46% year on year, so about 56 million at end-2009), against 662 million net new mobile subscriptions worldwide in 2008 (ITU, cited by grader B). Machines were at most a few percent of 2008 subscription growth, so read as a forecast it would be a miss. But the sentence is a conditional possibility: hedge word 'could', conditioned on 'sufficient collaboration and focus', and the chapter's bottom line frames machines as 'the major opportunity', not an expected outcome. Under D30 (and D27) a possibility-only claim is unfalsifiable: both outcomes agree with it. This differs from the 'may' claims graded elsewhere in this source (for example 2009-006), which state an expected outcome without a condition.

Observable by who holds the paying customers. Paid VoIP went to incumbents: Comcast's VoIP service made it the third-largest US home telephone provider, while Skype (the leading pure-play) remained a low-revenue business sold to Microsoft in 2011, a trade sale as the chapter advised. Mobile broadband went to LTE run by incumbent operators, not WiMAX entrants. Grader B's 'no horizon' objection: the chapter states a present-tense pattern for 2008 onward and the record is clear. Hit, medium confidence.

The graded part is usage frequency among GPS-phone owners. The nearest public measure is comScore M:Metrics (July 2008): 8% of US and 3% of European mobile subscribers accessed maps on the phone in the three months to May 2008, US up 82% and Europe up 49% year on year, mostly via the browser and for driving directions. Its base is all subscribers, not GPS-phone owners, the leading US device (the original iPhone) had no GPS, and it gives reach, not frequency; using it would grade a different quantity (D23). Looked for 2008 comScore, Nielsen Mobile, Berg Insight and J.D. Power usage figures among GPS-handset owners; none found in public. Stays ungradable.

The forecast is a causal one: that communications tools differentiate sites competitively. Grader A shows sites added tools (Facebook Chat released April 2008) and that Facebook led MySpace, but no source links share changes to communications features; that is a proxy (D23). No measure of the differentiator effect was found. Ungradable.

The captured quote is the literal sentence, and it happened: at Mobile World Congress 2008 Ericsson demonstrated the first end-to-end LTE call on a handheld and Motorola demonstrated LTE equipment and HD streaming. Grader B's second reading (the chapter's doubt about demand for speed) is a different sentence of the chapter, not the captured claim, so it does not create a competing reading of this claim. Hit, near-certain but low information.

One public estimate of the same quantity for 2009 was found: the global smart grid market at $69.3bn (with the US at $21.4bn), cited on Wikipedia. D23 makes a claim ungradable when estimates span more than a factor of 2; grader A asserted such a spread but cited no second global estimate, so the rule does not apply on the evidence. Against $69.3bn the forecast is 64% low: miss. Against the US-only figure it would be partial, but the edition is global. Low confidence: smart grid scope varies by source.

The core of the claim is an event (a significant expansion of the subsidy model in 2009), and it happened: from late 2008 and through 2009 major operators in the US and Europe sold netbooks at low or zero upfront price on mobile-broadband contracts, the 'cellphone-like contract deals' trend. 'Pervasive' is read as widely offered by operators, which held; no series gives the share of devices sold this way, so a share reading is not tested. Grader A's ungradable rests on the share reading only. Moderate-low confidence.

The quantity is measured by IDC's worldwide disk storage systems tracker. IDC reported full-year 2009 disk storage sales down 0.7% year over year (Q4 2009 up 0.2% to $7.3bn), after quarterly declines of up to 18% in H1 2009. Even the steepest quarterly fall is far from a halving; error well beyond 25%. Miss.

Two public estimates of the same quantity disagree: Gartner sales to end users 172.4m, +23.8%; IDC shipments 174.2m, +15.1% (from 151.4m in 2008). D23: grade against their median, 19.45%, which is under 20% and within 0.5 pt of a forecast of just under 20%: hit. Grader A used Gartner only, which D23 does not allow when a second estimate exists. Sub-parts went worse: all-phone growth was about -1% (Gartner), not +4%, and Gartner shows no 15-point fall in smartphone growth; the headline smartphone level is graded. Low confidence: the trackers straddle the threshold.

Not a page-access problem: no public series measures inbox checks per office worker per day for 2009. Radicati counts emails sent and received per business user, a different quantity (D23). Looked for a 2009 time-use or workplace survey of email checking frequency; none found.

The quantity is the share of unbranded/little-known brands in technology purchases in 2009; no public series was found. Grader A's evidence is that Vizio became North America's largest LCD TV seller by volume in 2007, before the target year and by then not an unknown brand; netbooks came mostly from established brands (Asus, Acer). Neither tests a 2009 shift. Ungradable.

Both graders read the claim as e-discovery revenue. The chapter is about the volume of lawsuits over digital matters (privacy, product claims, RSI, IP and copyright class actions), not about electronic discovery services, so e-discovery revenue is a different quantity (D23). For the record, on the graders' reading the Socha-Gelbmann surveys give 2007 commercial e-discovery revenue of $2.794bn (with a pre-recession projection of $4.051bn for 2009) and 2009 revenue of about $2.8bn: flat rather than falling, which a 'recession-proof' reading would call a hit and a 'kept growing' reading a stall; that reading is not graded. No public series counts digital-related litigation across these case types for 2008 and 2009. Looked for: Socha-Gelbmann public results 2008 to 2010, litigation trend surveys, patent and copyright filing counts (each covers only one slice). Stays ungradable.

Grader A named the right measure (McKinsey's 2009 Web 2.0 survey) but could not open it. Opened via the Internet Archive: the survey (fielded June 2009, about 1,700 executives) shows, in Exhibit 2, internal use of social networking by 42% of respondents at companies reporting benefits and 30% at companies reporting none, among only the 1,032 respondents whose companies use Web 2.0 internally; across all respondents that is well under half. McKinsey's 2010 survey reports 'significant increases' in the share of companies using social networking, to 40% (internal and external use), so 2009 was below 40% and rising. Growth in 2009 and adoption by a minority both held as stated. Hit. Grader B's Inc. 500 figure measured external social media, not internal networks.

The chapter is global ('Overall, in 2009 ... per viewer'). Eurodata TV Worldwide (89 countries): average daily viewing 3h12 in 2009, up 3 minutes on 2008, i.e. about 21 minutes a week. 30 is 43% above 21: miss. UK BARB via Ofcom (3.74 to 3.75 hours a day, about 4 minutes a week) is also a miss. Grader B's Nielsen figure is US Q1 only and is not the stated scope.

The claim names which challenge is 'fundamental'; that is a ranking of concerns, not an outcome, like the w1 adjudication of 2007-003 (a state of worry). Grader A's evidence is YouTube's 2007 'not material' revenue, two years before the target year, which does not test 2009. Ungradable.

The chapter's own test is that megastars 'may have to play arenas, not stadiums'. In 2009 the opposite happened: U2's 360 Tour opened in stadiums, sold 650,000 tickets in seven hours, and ended as the highest-grossing tour ever ($736m, 7.27 million tickets). Grader B looked for a premium series; the chapter's stadium-versus-arena test is observable. Miss.

Two public measures, in the two largest markets for the chapter's argument. UK: Ofcom's Communications Market Report 2010 (Figure 1.2) puts WiFi radio take-up at 2% of individuals in Q1 2010, while 15% listened to radio via the internet monthly, so sets were a small share of the audience. US: the Arbitron/Edison Infinite Dial 2010 has weekly online radio at 17% in both the early-2009 and early-2010 surveys (no growth over 2009), listening going to Internet-only services (Pandora) and computers, and a radio-like Internet radio device appearing only as an interest item (18% 'very interested'). WiFi sets were neither the biggest impetus nor a visible one in 2009. Miss. 'May' is Deloitte's usual pre-2010 voice for an expected outcome in this source and is graded as such (as in 2009-006).

The edition fixes the base: global mobile ad spend 'only $1 billion' at end-2008 (0.4% of global ad revenue). Gartner reported 2010 mobile ad revenue of US$1.6bn (forecasting more than double, US$3.3bn, for 2011), so 2009 was below US$1.6bn. 2.0 against at most 1.6 is 25% or more off: miss. Grader B's Gartner figures of US$1.7bn (2007) and US$2.7bn (2008 forecast) use an older, broader definition inconsistent with Deloitte's US$1bn base and with Gartner's own later series.

The event is confirmed on reputable sites in 2009 (The New York Times' ad feed served malicious ads 11-14 September 2009; the Guardian reported Internet companies facing the threat), but no source counts 'hundreds' of reputable sites in 2009. The direction and kind are right and the scale is unshown. Partial, low confidence.

Under D23 a conditional is graded if the condition held. Demand stayed strong (iPhone users about 400 MB a month against 40-80 MB for typical smartphones), and the stress was severe: AT&T's network in New York, San Francisco and other iPhone-heavy areas 'quickly bogged down', with failed calls and slow 3G, and AT&T invested billions and ended unlimited data in June 2010. Grader A's 'no measure of severity' is answered by the documented congestion. Hit.

Broadcast mobile TV closed region by region: Germany's MFD ended April 2008, Albania's DVB-H ended October 2010, Austria and Switzerland switched off around 2010, the Netherlands in 2011, Finland and Italy by 2012. Closures inside the two-year window count as a hit under D16; grader A's late-timing penalty applies only from year 3. 'Temporary' turned out permanent, which does not weaken the demise. Hit.

No public count of seats moved to VDI or thin client in 2010. IDC thin-client device shipments sit in paid trackers and are a different quantity from VDI seats (VDI also runs on repurposed PCs), so would be a proxy (D23). Earlier reason was paywalled analyst data, not a blocked page; no public press-release figure located.

The chapter is about sector performance in a recovery ('CleanTech makes a comeback'), so the investment reading dominates. Yahoo Finance monthly adjusted closes, re-fetched by the adjudicator: Guggenheim Solar ETF (TAN) 75.80 (Dec 2009) to 54.20 (Dec 2010), -28.5%; PowerShares WilderHill Clean Energy (PBW) 39.24 to 37.06, -5.6%. Solar underperformed the broad clean-energy index by about 23 points: hit. Grader A could not retrieve the index data.

A series exists and was retrieved: ZenithOptimedia put internet at 16.0% of global adspend in 2011 ($76.4bn). D18 rate: 15 - 16.0 = -1.0 pt, within 1.0: partial. Deloitte's 'roughly 10% at end-2009' base is lower than Zenith's, a baseline difference of the same quantity (D23). Grader B's ungradable was for lack of retrieval only.

IFPI Digital Music Report 2012 gives an estimated 8.2 million paying subscribers globally in 2010 (13.4 million in 2011). The 10 million threshold was not crossed in 2010; the forecast is 22% above the actual (10 vs 8.2), within 25%: partial under the D16 quantitative rule. Threshold crossed in 2011.

No source splits 2010 mobile search exactly, but two figures bracket it. Google, the dominant mobile search provider, said in October 2010 it was on track for US$1bn in mobile revenue that year (mostly search ads, some display). Gartner put all mobile advertising at US$1.6bn in 2010, with search and maps its largest category. Mobile search therefore fell roughly between US$0.8bn and US$1.6bn, within or at most about 20% below the stated range. Grader A was right that no exact split exists, but both bracket figures are of the same quantity or contain it. Hit, low-medium confidence.

The title names each device class, so the per-class reading is more faithful than grader B's combined smartphone-plus-tablet pool. By end-2011 Android passed 50% of quarterly smartphone sales (Q4 2011, Gartner) with a lead of more than 25 points over the next OS, and iPad held 61.5% of tablet shipments in Q3 2011 (IDC). Each class had a dominant OS at the target date: miss. Medium confidence on where 'dominant' starts.

No public series splits 2011 tablet purchases by enterprise vs consumer buyer. IDC/Gartner commercial-vs-consumer splits for 2011 are in paid trackers; no public press-release figure for the 2011 enterprise share was located. Total tablet shipments are a different quantity (D23).

Eurostat's enterprise e-government series is the matching measure. With archive access, the 2010 reference-year values were found (Jan 2011 survey, EU27: 74% obtaining information, 76% downloading forms, 69% returning completed forms), which match Deloitte's 75% baseline. No 2011 reference-year value was found: the Eurostat datasets (tin00107, isoc_bde15ei) are no longer disseminated, the archived Statistics Explained pages stop at 2010, and the 2012 ICT-usage-in-enterprises Statistics in Focus carries no e-government figure. The only year-before value is the claim's own baseline, so grading against it would test nothing. Ungradable for 2011; low certainty, a 2011 OECD or Eurostat figure may exist offline.

The claim is comparative ('more ... than ever before'); both graders cite only 2011 events (Wikipedia PSN breach, cookie directive) with no measure against 2010, itself a peak privacy year (Facebook settings, Street View Wi-Fi). Evidence does not support any verdict on the comparison.

The claim is a rate threshold, graded under D18, not the D16 placement windows grader B applied (late arrival 3-5 years is a placement rule, not a numeric one). US DVR penetration was 32% (2009) and 38% (2010); at that pace about 44% at end-2011, and the edition itself put the US crossing in 2011-2012. No source shows the US near 50% in 2011, so the US is more than 1 pt short and the two-market claim fails: miss. TV advertising was little affected, as stated, but the headline is the penetration number. Medium confidence: no retrieved 2011 US figure; 2011 is extrapolated by both graders.

No series measures 3D printers as a segment of the power-tools or industrial-manufacturing markets. Wohlers total additive-manufacturing revenue is a different quantity (D23). Not a page-access gap: even with Wohlers open, the named segment is unmeasured.

Scope is global and the window is 24 hours. National panels (BARB UK, Nielsen US) publish live vs time-shifted within 7 days (BARB) or Live+SD/+3/+7 (Nielsen), not a global or 24-hour share. Ofcom access would only add UK 7-day data, a different window and scope. Ungradable stays.
Only analyst estimates (IHS, ABI, Juniper, Berg) of NFC device or handset shipments exist, in paid reports with differing device scopes; no public 2012 actual was located. Not a blocked-page case.

Cisco VNI release (June 2014) gives 33% of IP traffic from non-PC devices, but IP traffic includes managed IPTV/VoD to set-top boxes; the claim is about Internet traffic. The release has no Internet-only device split, and removing managed video plausibly puts the PC share near 80%, so the miss rests on an unconfirmed figure.

Deloitte's 2011 baseline ($1.5bn) is Massolution's $1.47bn. The same series gives $2.66bn for 2012 and, in the 2015CF report, $6.1bn for 2013 ($16.2bn in 2014, +167%). $3bn is 51% below: miss. The $2.8bn for 2013 on Wikipedia (journalism passage) has no stated source or scope and sits barely above the same series' 2012 value, so it is not treated as an estimate of the same quantity; the D23 factor-2 rule is not triggered. Grader B's $6.1bn was from memory; it is now retrieved via the Massolution release. Medium-low confidence.

Earlier adjudication stands: no public global installed-base figure for 2013; available figures are US-only (25m households in 2012) or 2019 (1.26bn connected TVs). Building a base from shipment shares is a constructed estimate (D23). Likely exceeded, but not measured.
No tracker publishes tablet installed base by screen size; deriving it from shipments needs replacement assumptions (proxy, D23). Not a page-access gap.

The event can be dated: Germany's AGF restructured in 2017 so that streaming data enter the ratings measurement; in the UK, BARB's fusion of panel and device data (Dovetail) is documented only for later years, not 2014. Neither market shows hybrid ratings in 2014 or within 2 years in the evidence; Germany's came 3 years after the placed year, which D16 grades partial. Low confidence: no retrieved launch date for BARB's hybrid, and an earlier German streaming pilot cannot be ruled out.

IFPI Digital Music Report 2015 (contemporaneous vintage): 2014 performance rights revenue $948m, +8.3%, on an amended scope that moved US SoundExchange to digital and gave US performance rights a nil value. $1bn vs $948m is 5.5% off: hit under the D16 quantitative rule (within 10%). On the scope in force when Deloitte forecast, IFPI's DMR 2014 already put 2013 at $1.1bn (+19%), so the threshold was crossed on that basis too (early arrival not penalised). Both vintages give hit; the threshold-not-crossed reading on the new scope is the only weakness. Grader B's 'factor 2 spread' rested on a later restatement not used here; vintages of the same quantity are gradable (D23).

The claim states a level (50bn a day) as well as a ratio. No aggregate of MIM traffic exists; per-app disclosures use different counts (WhatsApp reported 30bn a day by January 2015, while earlier WhatsApp figures counted sent and received separately, which differ by about a factor of 2), and WeChat, Messenger, LINE and iMessage gave no comparable 2014 counts. Estimates of the total therefore span more than a factor of 2 depending on the counting convention: ungradable under D23. Grader B's sum is a construction from partial disclosures. The ratio half very likely held (WhatsApp alone at or above the SMS level), noted but not graded alone.

The claim spans developed markets; only single-country surveys (Ofcom UK, Pew US) exist, with different age bands and growth bases (points vs percent). Opening Ofcom would give one country, not the stated scope. Not re-attempted beyond confirming no cross-market series.
No installed-base series of civil drones by price. FAA registrations began Dec 2015, cover the US only and all drones over 250 g. Not a page-access gap.

Gartner, the consensus series Deloitte cites (forecast 217,350 for 2015 in Oct 2014), later reported 219,168 units shipped in 2015 (in its 2016 forecast, 455,772 for 2016). 220,000 vs 219,168 is +0.4%: hit. Grader A did not retrieve the figure (403); grader B recalled it, now confirmed via search. Wohlers' desktop counts for 2015 are higher, but no Wohlers figure was retrieved, so the D23 median rule is applied to the one retrieved estimate. Medium confidence; a higher Wohlers count could move this to partial.

ITU (Nov 2022 vintage): fixed-broadband subscriptions 730.8m (2014) and 834.9m (2015). 715m is 14.4% below: within 25%, not 10%, partial; growth was about 14%, not 2%. Business lines are a minority of subscriptions; even removing 10% for them gives about 750m and a hit, but no residential series exists, so the graded figure is subscriptions, the same quantity with a stated scope difference (D23). Grader A's own figure (about 795m) is 10.1% above 715m, outside the 10% hit band, so its hit was an arithmetic error; its residential adjustment was unsourced. Speed sub-claim not graded.

Only bracketing market-research figures ($9m in 2012, about $380m in 2022) were found; 2016 estimates from market-research firms differ by scope (materials vs products) and span more than a factor of 2 (D23). Not resolved by page access.

SuperData put 2016 VR revenue at $1.8bn (games 44% of it), fetched by the adjudicator from VGChartz's report of the SuperData release. $1.0bn is 44% below: miss. Grader B fetched only SuperData's unit counts. Medium confidence; one estimate.

PageFair's 2017 Adblock Report (Dec 2016 data) counts 380 million mobile devices using adblock software on mobile browsers, up 108 million in 2016, 94% in Asia-Pacific. Against the edition's own base of 3.4 billion mobile devices that is about 11%, some 37 times the forecast; even if PageFair overstated by a factor of 10 the share would exceed 1%. Reading note: PageFair's mobile count is of adblocking browsers (UC Browser and similar), while the chapter frames ad-blockers as installed software and iOS content blockers; an adblocking browser is installed ad-blocking software on the device, so the plain reading 'use an ad-blocker' covers it, and the chapter does not exclude it. Miss.

Leichtman Research: about 82% of US TV households subscribed to pay TV in 2016 (fetched; 87% in 2011), 79% in 2017. D18: 81 - 82 = -1.0 pt, within 1.0: partial. Grader A's Pew figure is an adult base and was rightly set aside, but a household series was retrievable.

IDC: 163.5m tablets shipped in 2017, down 6.5% from 174.8m in 2016 (IDC table on Wikipedia, retrieved by the adjudicator). Under the 165m ceiling: hit. The 'down about 10% from 182m' part uses a different 2016 base than IDC's.

UK (BARB via Ofcom, ages 16-24, live plus 7-day): 2018 down 15% to 85 minutes a day (at the top of the band); 2019 down 18% to 70 minutes (outside the band, 20% beyond its 15% edge; H1 2019 was down 22%). A conjunctive band claim is capped by its worst measured component: the UK 2019 value is within 25% of the band edge, so at most partial. US (Nielsen) and Canada (Numeris) 18-24 series were not retrieved (Nielsen report pages give no data without the PDF; Numeris not public), so a larger US or Canadian decline could make this a miss. Low certainty.

The claim's base is people with internet access, not all adults. Pew: smartphone-dependent 20% of adults (Jan 2018 survey) and 17% (Feb 2019); internet users 89% and 90%. On the claim's base: 22.5% and 18.9%, which bracket 2018; the midpoint is about 20.7%, 0.7 pt off: partial (D18). Grader A graded on the all-adult base (20% exactly) although it noted the base difference: a reading error. Canada has no measure on this basis. Low confidence: single surveys move a lot year to year.
The headline quantity is industry revenue. Trackers (Canalys, Strategy Analytics) publish unit shipments; units times an assumed ASP is a proxy (D23). No public 2019 smart-speaker revenue measure.

Newzoo is the tracker. Via Wayback its Feb 2019 release was opened: it gives North America at $409.1m for 2019, but this is Newzoo's in-year forecast, and no 2018 North America base or 2019 actual was retrieved (2020 report pages and articles not archived at the URLs found; newzoo.com returns 403). A growth rate cannot be computed from one number. Ungradable; low certainty, the 2020 report would settle it.

Global radio revenue series (PwC Global Entertainment & Media Outlook) are paywalled and differ in scope (advertising only vs advertising plus licence fee and subscription). No public 2019 global figure on the same scope located.
CNNIC 43rd Statistical Report (retrieved by the adjudicator): mobile payment users reached 583 million at end-2018, up 10.7%. 600m is 2.9% above: hit. Grader B could not retrieve the report.
Deloitte's definition counts parts of chips; no tracker counts that quantity. AI-capable smartphone shares or vendor accelerator counts are proxies (D23).

GSA Dec 2020 update counts 259 companies deploying LTE or 5G (500+ incl. trials) with no 5G split; GSA's Aug 2021 release (Grader B's '120+ 5G projects') post-dates the target and says LTE was in 81% of networks in Oct 2020, implying well under 100 catalogued 5G at end-2020. No source confirms >100 companies testing 5G by end-2020.

2020 CDN market estimates come from market-research firms with paywalled reports and scopes that differ (security, video services); figures that circulate span widely. No same-scope public measure retrieved.
Trackers split AR/VR shipments by device type and, at most, consumer vs commercial in paid data; no public series of enterprise-plus-education headset sales. Not a page-access gap.
Newzoo's console segment excludes hardware; adding hardware needs unit times ASP assumptions (proxy, D23). No same-scope public measure.

Ofcom Media Nations (Barb in-home basis, recalculated for 2022): broadcaster content (live, recorded playback, BVoD) was 61% of video viewing in 2022, 57% in 2023 and 56% in 2024. The threshold event did not happen: 2022 was not the final year above 50%, and the share was still above half in 2024. On the D16 quantitative rule the stated path is 14% off in 2023 (49 vs 57) and 13% off in 2022 (53 vs 61), within 25%: partial. Ofcom's switch to in-home-only viewing moves shares by about a point (out-of-home added just under 2% to total viewing), which does not change the result. If the claim is read as a binary event, it is a miss; the edition gives explicit numbers, so the quantitative reading is used (same treatment as other threshold claims in this pass).

PitchBook counted US$7.8bn of global VC into semiconductor startups in 2022 (to 5 December), fetched from The Register. That is above the US$6bn floor: hit. PitchBook's 2021 figure (US$14.5bn) is higher than Deloitte's base, a method difference of the same quantity (D23), stated; the 'new highs' framing failed on PitchBook's series, but the stated threshold is the claim. Grader A found no figure; one was retrievable.

Ericsson Mobility Report June 2023 (text verified by the adjudicator): 'From 100 million at the end of 2022, FWA connections worldwide are projected to increase to 300 million by the end of 2028.' 88m is 12% below: within 25%, not 10%: partial.

No public annual Wi-Fi 6 device shipment actual for 2022 was found. Wi-Fi Alliance newsroom pages tried returned 404; IDC figures are forecasts or paywalled; chipset projections are a different quantity. Low certainty: a Wi-Fi Alliance or IDC public actual may exist.

IDC reports wearables by form (earwear, smartwatches, wristbands); Deloitte's 'health and wellness' scope matches none, and the two candidate scopes (all wearables about 500m; watches plus bands) give opposite verdicts. No same-scope measure (D23).

Estimates of end-2022 floating PV conflict: REN21 GSR 2024 'at least 5.6 GW operational' (5.2 is 7% below, a hit), REN21 GSR 2023 'well over 3 GW', Wikipedia/Bloomberg 13 GW (miss). Spread exceeds 2x (D23), so the agreed miss is not supported.

Graders' 2023 price evidence (itel P55 5G at Rs 9,699, ~US$116) returned 404; only Lava Blaze 5G (Oct 2022, ~US$125) and Poco C75 5G (Dec 2024, Rs 7,399 per Cashify) were confirmed. A 2023 phone within 10% of US$99 (with offers) would make it a hit, so partial rests on an unconfirmed figure.

Drake Star's gaming deal tracker: 163 M&A deals announced in 2023 (Q1 2023: 43). For 2022 its quarterly releases give Q4 2022 alone at 76 M&A deals, Q1 2022 at about 100 (387 transactions less 287 financings), and 132 PC/console and mobile M&A transactions in the first nine months; 2022 M&A count was therefore well above 200, and total gaming deals fell from 1,300+ (2022) to 960 (2023). The count fell by roughly a quarter or more instead of rising 25%: miss. Drake Star itself describes 2023 deal activity as shifting back to pre-COVID levels. The exact 2022 M&A total sits in the gated PDF; the direction is not in doubt.

USGS (verified): China's gallium exports recovered in 2024 as licences were granted; prices rose (to $420/kg by October) 'as stocks outside of China depleted further'; China banned gallium exports to the US only in December 2024. Supply tightened and stocks ran down, but with exports flowing again there is no evidence of an actual shortfall in multiple regions during 2024. Partly happened: partial. Moderate-low confidence on what counts as 'running short'.

Every iPhone 14 or later supports satellite messaging (Apple). IDC puts Apple's 2025 shipments at 247.4m, +6.1%, so about 233m in 2024; the iPhone 13 and SE, the only non-satellite iPhones on sale in 2024, were the cheap tail of the line. Satellite-capable Huawei Mate 60 and Pura 70 and Pixel 9 models add to that. This counts units of the same quantity (satellite-capable phones), not a proxy of another quantity, so D23 does not bar it. Even with 15% of iPhones non-satellite the total is above 200m, and D16 allows a hit down to 180m. Medium confidence: no tracker count retrieved; the Apple 2025 figure is from IDC's release title.

The claim has two observable parts and both held. Industry collaboration on content provenance was active in 2025: the C2PA coalition (Adobe, Amazon, BBC, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Sony, TikTok and others) runs Content Credentials as a cross-industry standard. Detection evasion is the documented pattern. It was partly in place before 2025, and D16 does not penalise early arrival. Grader A's ungradable treats it as an unmeasurable pattern, but its parts are events, which are gradable. Moderate confidence: 'at least some' is a low bar.
Counterpoint (fetched): global smartphone shipments grew 2% in 2025; IDC preliminary 1.9%. D18: about 5 pt below: miss. Grader B could not retrieve tracker releases.

2025 actuals for silicon photonics chips (not modules) are not yet public; analyst figures (Yole, LightCounting) are paywalled, forecast-based and scope modules or PICs differently, spanning more than a factor of 2 (D23).
